messages.text: Do we qualify for any state assistance programs? Family of four.

I can help check. I need a few details first.

1. Who is in your household of four? Please tell me each person's age. Also tell me if anyone is pregnant, recently had a baby, or has a disability.
2. What is each person's income before taxes? Tell me how often it's paid (weekly, every two weeks, or monthly). Please also say where it comes from, like a job, Social Security, or unemployment.

Once I have this, I'll look up the current Tennessee and federal rules and check food assistance (SNAP), WIC, and TennCare/CoverKids.

Me, my wife, and our two kids. I'm 44, she's 42, kids are 12 and 9. Nobody's pregnant, no recent babies, no disabilities.

We both have jobs with salaries. Together we bring in about $9,000 a month before taxes. Paid monthly, I think, or twice a month? Not sure exactly. Both paychecks come from regular jobs, nothing else.

**It looks unlikely that your family qualifies for any of these programs at about $9,000 a month before taxes.** You can still apply. Only the agency can decide, and I can't promise an outcome.

**Health coverage for your kids (TennCare or CoverKids)**
- **TennCare for kids ages 6 to 18:** The limit for a family of four is about $3,658 a month before taxes. Your income is well above that, so TennCare looks **unlikely**.
- **CoverKids:** The limit for a family of four is about $6,875 a month before taxes. Your income is above that too, so CoverKids also looks **unlikely**.
- Both numbers come from Tennessee's [TennCare/CoverKids Eligibility Reference Guide](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html). I opened that page.
- **Parents:** I didn't find a limit for adults on that page, so I can't say anything about your coverage.

**Food assistance (SNAP)**
- **Unlikely under either rule:** Tennessee's limit is unsettled. Some sources say 130% of the poverty level, and others say 200%.
  - At 130%, secondary websites list about $3,575 a month for a family of four.
  - At 200%, the limit would be about $5,500 a month.
  - Your income is above both.
- **Sources:** USDA's own 2026-27 page wouldn't open for me, so the 130% figure comes from websites that repeat USDA's numbers. I did not open them. The $5,500 is my own math: 200% of a $33,000 poverty level for four people, divided by 12. I also did not open a page for that $33,000 figure.
- **Deductions:** Rent, child care, and utilities can lower the income SNAP counts. They would have to cut it by thousands of dollars a month to matter in your case, so I don't expect them to change the result.

**WIC**
- WIC is for pregnant women, new mothers, babies, and children under 5. Based on what you told me, no one in your family fits that. I didn't look up WIC rules this time.

**If you want to check anyway**
- **SNAP:** Apply online at the [One DHS portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp) or call 1-833-772-8347. The [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html) has the details.
- **TennCare or CoverKids:** Call TennCare at 1-855-259-0701. That number came up in my search results, and I didn't confirm it on an official page.
- **Free local help:** Call **211**.

**One thing to double-check:** Is the $9,000 before taxes? If your real income is lower, for example if some of it is bonus pay or it dropped recently, tell me and I'll check again.

Sources:
- [TennCare Eligibility Reference Guide](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
yep, $9k before taxes, both salaries. no bonuses or anything like that, and nothing's dropped recently.

Thanks for confirming. That means my answer stays the same. At about $9,000 a month before taxes for a family of four, all three programs look **unlikely**.

- **TennCare for your kids:** The limit is about $3,658 a month. You're well over it.
- **CoverKids:** The limit is about $6,875 a month. You're over it.
- **Food assistance (SNAP):** Even the higher limit that some sources report, about $5,500 a month, is below your income.
- **WIC:** No one in your family fits the groups it serves.

You can still apply. Only the agency can decide, and rules can change. You could also have costs I haven't counted, like child care or large medical bills. They almost certainly wouldn't close a gap this big, but the caseworker can check.

If you want to try:
- **SNAP:** [One DHS portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp) or 1-833-772-8347.
- **TennCare or CoverKids:** 1-855-259-0701.
- **Free local help:** Call **211**. They can point you to food banks, health clinics, and other help that doesn't depend on income limits.

If your situation changes, like a job loss or a pay cut, come back and I'll look again.

Sources:
- [TennCare Eligibility Reference Guide](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)

Links: [{"title":"Key Takeaways","url":"https://sycamoretn.org/snap-in-tn/"},{"title":"The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in Tennessee","url":"https://sycamoretn.org/?p=17208"},{"title":"State of Tennessee Food Stamp Calculator","url":"https://voip.puri.sm/?p=1240157"},{"title":"Do I Qualify for SNAP in Tennessee?","url":"https://daycarecalc.com/snap-eligibility/tennessee"},{"title":"tennessee snap eligibility 2026","url":"https://benefitsusa.org/en/blog/tennessee-snap-eligibility-2026"},{"title":"State of Tennessee Food Stamp Calculator","url":"https://cvs.pantherdb.org/?p=1236422"},{"title":"snapeligibilitycalculator.com","url":"https://snapeligibilitycalculator.com/?p=4077"},{"title":"snap shakeup could put more food on memphis tables","url":"https://hoodline.com/2026/06/snap-shakeup-could-put-more-food-on-memphis-tables/"},{"title":"the supplemental nutrition assistance program snap in tennessee","url":"https://sycamoretn.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/the-supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap-in-tennessee.pdf"}]

The search turned up conflicting figures, so I'd verify with Tennessee DHS before relying on any single number.

**Gross limit, 130% of poverty (most authoritative-looking figures):**
- BenefitsUSA lists $3,575 per month and $42,900 per year for a household of 4, with figures that apply from October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026.
- Sycamore Institute gives a lower figure, saying the gross limit cannot exceed 130% of poverty—or $3,483 for a family of four.
- A third source gives $3,250 for a household of 4, which implies an older poverty base.

**Possible change to 200% of poverty:**
- A June 2026 report says the Tennessee Department of Human Services has adopted broad‑based categorical eligibility (BBCE). That move raises the SNAP gross‑income threshold from 130% to 200% of total household gross monthly income and removes asset limits for some households.
- DayCareCalc says Tennessee uses broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), which means the gross income limit is 200% of the federal poverty level. It gives $5,200/month for a family of 4 and recommends contacting Tennessee DHS to confirm current thresholds.
- Sycamore's earlier piece said the BBCE change was pending approval from the Tennessee General Assembly, so its status may have changed since.

**Net limit, 100% of poverty:** Figures range from $2,680 for a family of four (Sycamore) to $2,750 (BenefitsUSA) and $2,500 (the third source).

**Bottom line:** Under the 130% rule, the monthly gross limit for a family of 4 is roughly $3,250–$3,575 depending on the source's poverty base. If Tennessee has adopted BBCE, the limit would be about $5,200. The sources don't agree on which rule is in effect, so the official TDHS thresholds for October 2026 onward should be checked directly.

- **Gross income test:** For households without an elderly or disabled member, TDHS applies a gross income cap set at 130 percent of the poverty guideline, compared against the limit for the household's size (a gross income limit of one hundred thirty (130) percent of the poverty level income standard). Policy 24.14 governs the monthly gross and net standards, and that document says the gross standard does not apply to households that contain elderly or disabled household members.
- **Categorical eligibility:** Tennessee's version is narrower than the broad-based approach. It covers households whose members all receive SSI or Families First, plus extended eligibility for certain Family Focused Solutions recipients (Households consisting entirely of Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and/or Families First (FF) recipients are categorically eligible for SNAP.). Categorically eligible households are not subject to the SNAP resource limit or the net and gross income limits.
- **Exclusions:** Categorical eligibility is not available if a member has an Intentional Program Violation disqualification, or for certain ineligible aliens, ineligible students, people disqualified for voluntary quit or work requirements, and institutionalized individuals (Categorical eligibility does not apply to households who: a. have a member(s) who is disqualified for an Intentional Program Violation).

**Caveats:** Several of these documents are dated (some were last reviewed in 2023 and others date to 2018 or earlier), and the poverty-level dollar table wasn't captured in the results. Confirm current gross and net figures against the latest TDHS income standards or the USDA FNS SNAP income tables before relying on them.

The FY 2027 standards for a four-person household in the 48 contiguous states and D.C. are consistent across the sources: a $3,575 gross monthly limit (130% of poverty) and a $2,750 net monthly limit (100% of poverty), effective October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027.

- **Gross limit:** Several sources give $3,575 for four, including the standard gross limit (130% of poverty) becomes $1,729 a month for one person and $3,575 for four.
- **Net limit:** Net income limit (100% of poverty): $1,330 for one, $1,804 for two, $2,277 for three, $2,750 for four.
- **Year-over-year change:** The FY 2026 four-person figures were $3,483 gross and $2,680 net, per a comparison table showing the FY2026 gross limit for four people at $3,483 and the FY2027 limit at $3,575.
- **Elderly or disabled households:** One source notes that households with a member who is 60 or older or disabled only have to meet the net limit. Another lists a separate elderly/disabled separate household (165% FPL) screen, at $4,538 for four.
- **Alaska and Hawaii:** These have higher standards. Alaska gross for a household of four is $4,469 and net is $3,438; Hawaii gross is $4,112 and net is $3,163.
- **State rules:** State categorical-eligibility policies can affect how financial screening works. Some states use broad-based categorical eligibility, which can change how the gross test applies.

Caveats: Most of these figures come from secondary websites, not the USDA Food and Nutrition Service. One DC government page (dhs.dc.gov) lists the FY 2027 period but its table content was not visible in the results, so I could not confirm its numbers. A projected-figures page predicted the same $3,575 and $2,750, but it was written before the official memo, so I'd treat it as lower-weight. For an authoritative citation, check the USDA FNS FY 2027 COLA memo directly.

Thanks for confirming. That means my answer stays the same. At about $9,000 a month before taxes for a family of four, all three programs look **unlikely**.

- **TennCare for your kids:** The limit is about $3,658 a month. You're well over it.
- **CoverKids:** The limit is about $6,875 a month. You're over it.
- **Food assistance (SNAP):** Even the higher limit that some sources report, about $5,500 a month, is below your income.
- **WIC:** No one in your family fits the groups it serves.

You can still apply. Only the agency can decide, and rules can change. You could also have costs I haven't counted, like child care or large medical bills. They almost certainly wouldn't close a gap this big, but the caseworker can check.

If you want to try:
- **SNAP:** [One DHS portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp) or 1-833-772-8347.
- **TennCare or CoverKids:** 1-855-259-0701.
- **Free local help:** Call **211**. They can point you to food banks, health clinics, and other help that doesn't depend on income limits.

If your situation changes, like a job loss or a pay cut, come back and I'll look again.

Sources:
- [TennCare Eligibility Reference Guide](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
